questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Pressure-specific azeotrope data reverse the first-vapour enrichment direction
questions.syllabus_anchor: Solutions: vapour composition; azeotropes
questions.question: A binary liquid has a minimum-boiling azeotrope at mole fraction xA=0.40 at pressure P1 and xA=0.60 at P2. Measurements on a liquid of xA=0.50 give vapour yA=0.46 at P1 and yA=0.55 at P2. For the first small vapour sample, which statement follows directly from these data?
options: A) It has the feed composition at both pressures because azeotropes cannot depend on pressure
B) It is enriched in A at P1 and depleted in A at P2
C) It is pure B at P1 and pure A at P2
D) It is depleted in A at P1 and enriched in A at P2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Relative to the 0.50 feed, 0.46 is depleted and 0.55 is enriched.
Step 1: At P1, \[y_A-x_A=0.46-0.50=-0.04.\] Thus the first vapour contains a smaller mole fraction of A than the liquid.
Step 2: At P2, \[y_A-x_A=0.55-0.50=+0.05.\] The direction reverses. At neither pressure is the given feed itself at its listed azeotropic composition.
Why: The phase compositions are measured at the specified pressure. A constant-boiling composition at one pressure is not a universal composition fixed for every pressure.
Why not the others: (A) It contradicts both measured vapour compositions and the stated pressure-dependent azeotropes. (B) It reverses the signs of both differences. (C) Neither 0.46 nor 0.55 is a pure-component mole fraction.
Key point: Compare vapour with its own liquid at the same pressure before inferring enrichment.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Fuel-cell charge stoichiometry and measured-voltage heat budget
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electrochemistry: fuel cells; Thermodynamics: enthalpy and work
questions.question: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell consumes hydrogen completely, has 100 percent Faradaic efficiency, and delivers a constant terminal voltage of 1.00 V. Formation of one mole liquid water releases 286 kJ enthalpy. Take F=96500 C mol−1 and neglect other energy stores. When 2F charge passes, what are the oxygen consumption and heat released to the surroundings at constant pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Oxygen consumption is 0.500 mol and heat release is 93 kJ.
Given: Charge 2F passes at terminal voltage 1.00 V.
Formula/Principle: Electrical work is QV; reaction enthalpy supplies electrical work plus heat.
Step 1: \[\ce{H2}+\tfrac12\ce{O2}\longrightarrow\ce{H2O(l)}\] transfers two moles of electrons per mole of hydrogen. Charge 2F therefore consumes 1 mol H2 and 0.5 mol O2.
Step 2: Delivered electrical work is \[W_{out}=QV=(2\times96500)(1.00)=193000\ \mathrm{J}=193\ \mathrm{kJ}.\]
Step 3: The released enthalpy is partitioned into electrical work and heat: \[Q_{out}=286-193=93\ \mathrm{kJ}.\]
Why: Reaction enthalpy is not identical to terminal electrical output. Both must be included in the constant-pressure energy budget.
Why not the others: (A) It doubles the oxygen demand. (C) It ignores the energy delivered electrically. (D) It both doubles oxygen and calls the electrical output heat.
Key point: Use electron stoichiometry before splitting chemical energy into work and heat.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Order identification from successive unequal halving intervals and fresh-sample prediction
questions.syllabus_anchor: Chemical Kinetics: integrated rate equations; half-life
questions.question: A reaction has one constant rate law over the stated concentration range. The concentration falls from 0.80 to 0.40 M in 10 min, then from 0.40 to 0.20 M in a further 5 min. Among zero-, first- and second-order models, which model fits both intervals, and what concentration does it predict after 4 min for a fresh 0.30 M sample at the same temperature?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Constant absolute consumption gives zero order and 0.14 M.
Given: Successive halving intervals are 10 and 5 min.
Formula/Principle: Zero-order concentration decreases linearly; first-order half-life is concentration independent.
Step 1: Interval rates are \[(0.80-0.40)/10=0.040,\qquad(0.40-0.20)/5=0.040\ \mathrm{M\,min^{-1}}.\] Both agree with concentration-independent rate. First-order halving times would be equal; second-order halving times would increase as concentration falls.
Step 2: For the fresh sample, \[[A]_t=[A]_0-kt=0.30-0.040(4)=0.14\ \mathrm M.\]
Why: Comparing successive halving intervals identifies how rate changes with concentration before extrapolating another initial condition.
Why not the others: (B) First order contradicts the unequal halving times. (C) Second order predicts the opposite halving-time trend. (D) It subtracts only 0.04 M rather than the four-minute consumption of 0.16 M.
Key point: Equal amounts per time and equal fractions per time imply different orders.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Buffered protonation coupled to a two-anion solubility product
questions.syllabus_anchor: Equilibrium: solubility product; common-ion and pH effects
questions.question: An idealised sparingly soluble salt MA2 has Ksp=1.0×10−12, with M2+ and A− as its dissolution ions. A large buffer fixes [H+]=Ka=1.0×10−3 M for HA, so protonation of dissolved A− does not change the buffer pH. No A is initially present. Ignore metal hydrolysis, complexation and activity corrections. What is the molar solubility of MA2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The solubility is 1.0×10−4 M.
Given: A fixed buffer has [H+]=Ka and dissolved salt supplies two anions per metal.
Formula/Principle: Combine acid dissociation, anion balance and the free-ion solubility product.
Step 1: \(K_a=[H^+][A^-]/[HA]\) and \([H^+]=K_a\) imply \([A^-]=[HA]\). Thus half the dissolved anion remains free.
Step 2: If solubility is s, \([M^{2+}]=s\) and total anion \([A^-]+[HA]=2s\). Hence free \([A^-]=s\).
Step 3: \[K_{sp}=[M^{2+}][A^-]^2=s^3=10^{-12},\quad s=10^{-4}\ \mathrm M.\]
Why: Only free ions enter the solubility product; analytical anion concentration includes protonated HA. The two-anion stoichiometry must still be conserved.
Why not the others: (A) It does not satisfy either ion balance or the cubic solubility relation. (B) It takes a square root as for a 1:1 salt. (D) It halves the solved solubility a second time after protonation was already included.
Key point: Couple protonation equilibrium to salt stoichiometry before evaluating Ksp.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Parameter degeneration of a translated conic into crossing lines
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordinate Geometry: conic sections; straight lines
questions.question: For which real k does \(x^2-y^2-2x+2y+k=0\) represent two intersecting straight lines, and where do those lines meet?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) k=0; (1,1).
Given: \(x^2-y^2-2x+2y+k=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(X^2-Y^2+k=0\ \text{is a pair of lines}\iff k=0\)
Step 1: \(x^2-2x=(x-1)^2-1,\quad-(y^2-2y)=-(y-1)^2+1\)
Step 2: \((x-1)^2-(y-1)^2+k=0\)
Step 3: \(k=0:\ (x-1)^2=(y-1)^2\Rightarrow(x-y)(x+y-2)=0\)
Step 4: \(x=y,\ x+y=2\Rightarrow x=1,\ y=1\)
Worked derivation: \[k=0,\qquad(x-y)(x+y-2)=0,\qquad\text{meeting point }(1,1)\]
Check: \[(1,1):\ 1-1-2+2+0=0;\quad\Delta=abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2=-k-1+1=-k=0\]
Why: \(k\ne0\Rightarrow(x-1)^2-(y-1)^2=-k\ne0\ \text{(hyperbola)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \((0,0):\ x-y=0\ \text{but}\ x+y-2=-2\ne0\); (C) \(k=1\ne0\); (D) \(k=-1\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{complete the squares first; the lines meet at the centre}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reconstruct a circle from orthogonality and two incidence constraints
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordinate Geometry: circles; perpendicular lines
questions.question: A circle passes through (1,0) and (0,2) and intersects the unit circle centred at the origin orthogonally. What are its centre and radius?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (1,5/4); 5/4.
Given: \(\text{circle through }(1,0),(0,2);\quad\text{orthogonal to }x^2+y^2=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{orthogonal circles}:\ d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2\Rightarrow h^2+k^2=r^2+1\)
Step 1: \((h-1)^2+k^2=r^2\Rightarrow h^2+k^2-2h+1=r^2\)
Step 2: \((r^2+1)-2h+1=r^2\Rightarrow h=1\)
Step 3: \(h^2+(k-2)^2=r^2\Rightarrow h^2+k^2-4k+4=r^2\)
Step 4: \((r^2+1)-4k+4=r^2\Rightarrow k=\tfrac54\)
Worked derivation: \[r^2=h^2+k^2-1=1+\tfrac{25}{16}-1=\tfrac{25}{16}\Rightarrow r=\tfrac54\]
Check: \[(0-1)^2+\left(2-\tfrac54\right)^2=1+\tfrac9{16}=\tfrac{25}{16};\quad(1-1)^2+\left(0-\tfrac54\right)^2=\tfrac{25}{16}\]
Why: \(\text{radii to a common point are perpendicular}\Rightarrow\text{Pythagoras on the centres}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac{\sqrt{41}}4=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}=d\ne r\); (C) \((0-1)^2+(2-\tfrac34)^2=\tfrac{41}{16}\ne\tfrac9{16}\); (D) \((1-0)^2+(0-1)^2=2\ne1\).
Key point: \(d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2\ \text{for orthogonal circles}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Unequal inverse endpoints in the area between a monotone graph and its inverse
questions.syllabus_anchor: Integral Calculus: area; inverse functions
questions.question: Let f(x)=x²+x on [0,1] and let g:[0,2]→[0,1] be its inverse. What is the area between y=f(x) and y=g(x) for 0≤x≤1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (17-5√5)/12.
Given: \(f(x)=x^2+x\ \text{on}\ [0,1],\quad g=f^{-1}\ \text{on}\ [0,2]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1g(y)\,dy=a\cdot1-\int_0^af(x)\,dx,\quad f(a)=1;\qquad A=\int_0^1(f-g)\,dx\)
Step 1: \(a^2+a=1\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}2\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(x^2+x)\,dx=\tfrac13+\tfrac12=\tfrac56\)
Step 3: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1g=a-\frac{a^3}3-\frac{a^2}2\)
Step 4: \(a^2=1-a,\quad a^3=a-a^2=2a-1\)
Step 5: \(A=\tfrac56-a+\dfrac{2a-1}3+\dfrac{1-a}2=\left(\tfrac56-\tfrac13+\tfrac12\right)+a\left(-1+\tfrac23-\tfrac12\right)=1-\tfrac{5a}6\)
Worked derivation: \[A=1-\frac56\cdot\frac{\sqrt5-1}2=\frac{12-5\sqrt5+5}{12}=\frac{17-5\sqrt5}{12}\approx0.485\]
Check: \[f(x)-x=x^2\ge0\Rightarrow f\ge x\ge g\ \text{on}\ [0,1];\quad0<0.485<\tfrac56\]
Why: \(g\ \text{reaches}\ 1\ \text{only at}\ y=2;\ \text{on}\ [0,1]\ \text{its graph mirrors}\ f\ \text{on}\ [0,a]\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac{5\sqrt5-7}{12}\approx0.348\ne0.485\); (B) \(\tfrac12\ne0.485\); (D) \(\tfrac56=\int_0^1f\ \text{only}\).
Key point: \(\text{match the endpoints of the inverse before using the reflection identity}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Rational half-angle substitution without a spurious endpoint pole
questions.syllabus_anchor: Integral Calculus: substitutions; trigonometric integrals
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(t=\tan\tfrac x2:\quad\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2},\quad dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}\)
Step 1: \(x=0\Rightarrow t=0;\quad x=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow t=1\)
Step 2: \(1+\sin x=\dfrac{1+t^2+2t}{1+t^2}=\dfrac{(1+t)^2}{1+t^2}\)
Step 3: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{1+t^2}{(1+t)^2}\cdot\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}=\int_0^1\frac{2\,dt}{(1+t)^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\left[-\frac2{1+t}\right]_0^1=-1+2=1\]
Check: \[\frac1{1+\sin x}=\sec^2x-\sec x\tan x\Rightarrow\left[\tan x-\sec x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\lim_{x\to\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-1}{\cos x}-(-1)=0+1=1\]
Why: \(\text{the integrand is continuous on}\ [0,\tfrac\pi2]\ \text{with values between}\ \tfrac12\ \text{and}\ 1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac\pi2=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx\); (B) \(2=\int_0^12\,dt\); (C) \(\tfrac12=\int_0^1\tfrac{dt}{(1+t)^2}\).
Key point: \(1+\sin x=\dfrac{(1+t)^2}{1+t^2}\ \text{with}\ t=\tan\tfrac x2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Normal-intercept range with a singular excluded parameter
questions.syllabus_anchor: Applications of Derivatives: normals; extrema
questions.question: For y=x², consider its normals at points (t,t²) with t≠0. What is the set of their y-intercepts, and is its greatest lower bound attained by one of these normals?
options: D) All real numbers; no finite lower bound
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (1/2,∞); not attained.
Given: \(y=x^2,\quad\text{normal at}\ (t,t^2),\ t\ne0\)
Formula/Principle: \(m_{\text{tangent}}=2t,\quad m_{\text{normal}}=-\dfrac1{2t}\)
Step 1: \(y-t^2=-\dfrac1{2t}(x-t)\)
Step 2: \(x=0:\ b(t)=t^2+\dfrac t{2t}=t^2+\tfrac12\)
Step 3: \(t\ne0\Rightarrow t^2\in(0,\infty)\Rightarrow b\in(\tfrac12,\infty)\)
Worked derivation: \[\{b(t):t\ne0\}=\left(\tfrac12,\infty\right),\qquad\inf b=\tfrac12\ \text{(only at}\ t=0\text{, excluded)}\]
Check: \[t=1:\ y-1=-\tfrac12(x-1)\Rightarrow y(0)=\tfrac32=1^2+\tfrac12\]
Why: \(t^2>0\ \text{strictly, and}\ t^2\to0^+\ \text{as}\ t\to0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(b=\tfrac12\iff t=0\ \text{(excluded)}\); (C) \(b\ge\tfrac12>0\); (D) \(b=t^2+\tfrac12>0\).
Key point: \(b(t)=t^2+\tfrac12\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Codomain restriction checked for well-definedness before bijection
questions.syllabus_anchor: Relations and Functions: domain; range; bijective functions
questions.question: The formula f(x)=x³-3x is restricted to domain [1,∞). Which is the smallest real codomain making f bijective, and what happens if that codomain is replaced by [0,∞) without changing the domain or formula?
options: A) [-2,∞); the proposed replacement is not a function into that codomain
C) [0,∞); the replacement is automatically onto
D) The real line; the replacement is one-to-one but not onto
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) [-2,∞); the proposed replacement is not a function into that codomain.
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-3x,\quad x\in[1,\infty)\)
Formula/Principle: \(f:D\to C\ \text{needs}\ f(D)\subseteq C;\quad\text{bijective}\iff\text{injective and}\ f(D)=C\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x^2-1)>0\ \text{for}\ x>1\Rightarrow\text{strictly increasing}\)
Step 2: \(f(1)=1-3=-2,\quad\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=\infty\)
Step 3: \(f([1,\infty))=[-2,\infty)\)
Worked derivation: \[C_{\min}=[-2,\infty);\qquad f(1)=-2\notin[0,\infty)\]
Check: \[f(2)=8-6=2,\quad f(\sqrt3)=0:\quad x\in[1,\sqrt3)\Rightarrow f(x)<0\]
Why: \(\text{an output outside the codomain means the rule is not a map into it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f(1)=-2\notin[0,\infty)\); (C) \([0,\infty)\not\supseteq f(D)\); (D) \((-\infty,-2)\ \text{is not attained}\Rightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{is not the smallest}\).
Key point: \(\text{check}\ f(D)\subseteq C\ \text{before asking about onto}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Shifted orthogonal matrix determinant selected by sign and trace
questions.syllabus_anchor: Matrices and Determinants: transpose; products; determinants
questions.question: A real 2×2 matrix X satisfies \(X+X^T+XX^T=3I\), tr X=0 and det(I+X)>0. What is det X?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3.
Given: \(X+X^T+XX^T=3I,\quad\operatorname{tr}X=0,\quad\det(I+X)>0,\quad X\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\det(I+X)=1+\operatorname{tr}X+\det X\ \ (2\times2)\)
Step 1: \((I+X)(I+X)^T=I+X+X^T+XX^T=I+3I=4I\)
Step 2: \(\det(I+X)^2=\det(4I)=4^2=16\)
Step 3: \(\det(I+X)>0\Rightarrow\det(I+X)=4\)
Worked derivation: \[4=1+0+\det X\Rightarrow\det X=3\]
Check: \[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\sqrt3\\\sqrt3&0\end{pmatrix}:\ X+X^T=0,\ XX^T=3I,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0,\ \det X=3\]
Why: \(\text{the sign condition removes}\ \det(I+X)=-4\)
Why not the others: (B) \(1+0+1=2\ne4\); (C) \(1+0+0=1\ne4\); (D) \(1+0-3=-2\ne4\).
Key point: \(Y=I+X\Rightarrow YY^T=4I\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Selection weights that preserve rather than assume conditional independence
questions.syllabus_anchor: Probability: conditional probability; independence; total probability
questions.question: Independent binary events X,Y have probabilities 1/2 and 1/3. A selection event S has probabilities 1, 1/2, 1/4 and q conditional on (X,Y) being (1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0), respectively. For what q are X and Y independent after conditioning on S, and then what is P(X|S)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) q=1/8; 4/5.
Given: \(P(X)=\tfrac12,\ P(Y)=\tfrac13\ \text{(independent)};\quad P(S\mid11,10,01,00)=1,\tfrac12,\tfrac14,q\)
Formula/Principle: \(w_{xy}=P(x,y)P(S\mid x,y);\quad X\perp Y\mid S\iff w_{11}w_{00}=w_{10}w_{01}\)
Step 1: \(w_{11}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13\cdot1=\tfrac16\)
Step 2: \(w_{10}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac16\)
Step 3: \(w_{01}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac1{24}\)
Step 4: \(w_{00}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot q=\tfrac q3\)
Step 5: \(\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac q3=\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac1{24}\Rightarrow q=\tfrac18,\quad w_{00}=\tfrac1{24}\)
Step 6: \(P(S)=\tfrac16+\tfrac16+\tfrac1{24}+\tfrac1{24}=\tfrac5{12}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(X\mid S)=\frac{\tfrac16+\tfrac16}{\tfrac5{12}}=\frac45\]
Check: \[P(Y\mid S)=\frac{\tfrac16+\tfrac1{24}}{\tfrac5{12}}=\frac12;\quad P(X,Y\mid S)=\frac{1/6}{5/12}=\frac25=\frac45\cdot\frac12\]
Why: \(\text{a }2\times2\text{ table factorises exactly when its cross-products are equal}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(q=\tfrac14:\ \tfrac1{72}\ne\tfrac1{144}\); (B) \(\tfrac23\ne\tfrac45\); (D) \(q=0:\ 0\ne\tfrac1{144}\).
Key point: \(\text{selection reweights the table; test}\ w_{11}w_{00}=w_{10}w_{01}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Trigonometric root coalescence at a parameter threshold
questions.syllabus_anchor: Trigonometric Functions: equations; graphs
questions.question: For distinct solutions x in [0,2π), consider \(\sin^2x-a\sin x=0\). What are the solution counts at a=1, a=1/2 and a=3/2, respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3,4,2.
Given: \(\sin^2x-a\sin x=0,\quad x\in[0,2\pi)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin x(\sin x-a)=0\Rightarrow\sin x=0\ \text{or}\ \sin x=a\)
Step 1: \(\sin x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pi\quad(2\ \text{roots for every}\ a)\)
Step 2: \(a=1:\ \sin x=1\Rightarrow x=\tfrac\pi2\quad(1\ \text{root})\Rightarrow N=3\)
Step 3: \(a=\tfrac12:\ x=\tfrac\pi6,\ \tfrac{5\pi}6\quad(2\ \text{roots})\Rightarrow N=4\)
Step 4: \(a=\tfrac32>1:\ \text{no root}\Rightarrow N=2\)
Worked derivation: \[\left(N(1),N(\tfrac12),N(\tfrac32)\right)=(3,4,2)\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac\pi6,\ a=\tfrac12:\ \tfrac14-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=0\]
Why: \(\text{distinct solutions are counted once, whatever their multiplicity}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(N(1)=2\ \text{omits}\ \tfrac\pi2\); (B) \(N(\tfrac12)=3\ \text{omits one of}\ \tfrac\pi6,\tfrac{5\pi}6\); (C) \(N(1)=4\ \text{counts}\ \tfrac\pi2\ \text{twice}\).
Key point: \(|a|>1\Rightarrow\sin x=a\ \text{has no solution}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Intercept-triangle area combined with distance to its plane
questions.syllabus_anchor: Three-dimensional Geometry: planes; distances
questions.question: A plane has equation x/2+y/3+z/6=1. Let A be the area of its intercept triangle with the positive coordinate axes and d its distance from the origin. What is Ad?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 18.
Given: \(\dfrac x2+\dfrac y3+\dfrac z6=1;\quad P(2,0,0),\ Q(0,3,0),\ R(0,0,6)\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\tfrac12|\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}|,\quad d=\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{l^2+m^2+n^2}}\ \text{for}\ lx+my+nz=c\)
Step 1: \(\vec{PQ}=(-2,3,0),\quad\vec{PR}=(-2,0,6)\)
Step 2: \(\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}=(3\cdot6-0,\ 0\cdot(-2)-(-2)\cdot6,\ 0-3\cdot(-2))=(18,12,6)\)
Step 3: \(A=\tfrac12\sqrt{324+144+36}=\tfrac12\sqrt{504}=3\sqrt{14}\)
Step 4: \(3x+2y+z=6\Rightarrow d=\dfrac6{\sqrt{9+4+1}}=\dfrac6{\sqrt{14}}\)
Worked derivation: \[Ad=3\sqrt{14}\cdot\frac6{\sqrt{14}}=18\]
Check: \[V_{OPQR}=\frac{2\cdot3\cdot6}6=6=\frac13Ad\Rightarrow Ad=18\]
Why: \(\sqrt{14}\ \text{cancels between the area and the distance}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(6\ne18\); (C) \(3\sqrt{14}=A\ \text{alone}\); (D) \(36=|\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}|\,d\ \text{(factor}\ \tfrac12\ \text{missing)}\).
Key point: \(Ad=3V=\dfrac{abc}2\ \text{for intercepts}\ a,b,c\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Orientation selects a scalar triple-product sign after norm decomposition
questions.syllabus_anchor: Vector Algebra: scalar and vector products; scalar triple product
questions.question: Unit vectors a,b are perpendicular. A vector c has |c|=3, c·a=1 and c·b=2. Its component along a×b is negative. What is \(\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) -2.
Given: \(|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=1,\ \mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=0,\ |\mathbf c|=3,\ \mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a=1,\ \mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=2,\ \mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)<0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf c=\alpha\mathbf a+\beta\mathbf b+\gamma(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b),\quad|\mathbf c|^2=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\)
Step 1: \(\alpha=\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a=1,\quad\beta=\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=2\)
Step 2: \(9=1+4+\gamma^2\Rightarrow\gamma=\pm2\)
Step 3: \(\gamma<0\Rightarrow\gamma=-2\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)\cdot\mathbf c=\gamma=-2\]
Check: \[\mathbf a=\hat i,\ \mathbf b=\hat j,\ \mathbf c=(1,2,-2):\ \begin{vmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&2&-2\end{vmatrix}=-2,\quad|\mathbf c|=3\]
Why: \(\mathbf a,\ \mathbf b,\ \mathbf a\times\mathbf b\ \text{form an orthonormal basis}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+2\Rightarrow\gamma>0\); (B) \(\gamma^2=5\Rightarrow|\mathbf c|^2=10\ne9\); (D) \(\gamma^2=9\Rightarrow|\mathbf c|^2=14\ne9\).
Key point: \([\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c]=\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reciprocal image of a line with a missing limiting point
questions.syllabus_anchor: Complex Numbers: geometric representation; reciprocals
questions.question: Let z range over the complex line Re z=2 and set w=1/z=u+iv. What is the exact locus of w?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (u-1/4)²+v²=1/16, excluding 0.
Given: \(\operatorname{Re}z=2,\quad w=\dfrac1z=u+iv\)
Formula/Principle: \(z=\dfrac1w=\dfrac{u-iv}{u^2+v^2}\)
Step 1: \(\operatorname{Re}z=\dfrac u{u^2+v^2}=2\)
Step 2: \(u^2+v^2-\dfrac u2=0,\quad(u,v)\ne(0,0)\)
Step 3: \(\left(u-\tfrac14\right)^2+v^2=\tfrac1{16}\)
Worked derivation: \[\left(u-\tfrac14\right)^2+v^2=\tfrac1{16},\qquad w\ne0\ \left(\tfrac1z\ne0\ \text{for every finite}\ z\right)\]
Check: \[z=2\Rightarrow w=\tfrac12:\ \left(\tfrac14\right)^2=\tfrac1{16};\quad z=2+2i\Rightarrow w=\tfrac{1-i}4:\ 0+\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac1{16}\]
Why: \(\text{multiplying by}\ u^2+v^2\ \text{adds the point}\ (0,0)\ \text{to the algebraic curve}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(w=\tfrac12:\ (\tfrac12-\tfrac12)^2+0=0\ne\tfrac14\); (B) \(w=0\ \text{is not a value of}\ \tfrac1z\); (C) \(z=2+2i\Rightarrow u=\tfrac14\ne\tfrac12\).
Key point: \(\text{inversion maps a line not through }0\text{ to a circle through }0\text{ with }0\text{ removed}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Closed-interval positivity versus global quadratic positivity
questions.syllabus_anchor: Quadratic Equations; Applications of Derivatives: extrema on intervals
questions.question: For which real a is \(x^2-2ax+2a\) strictly positive at every x in the closed interval [0,1]?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) a>0.
Given: \(q(x)=x^2-2ax+2a>0\ \ \forall x\in[0,1]\)
Formula/Principle: \(q(x)=(x-a)^2+2a-a^2;\quad\text{vertex at}\ x=a\)
Step 1: \(a\le0:\ q(0)=2a\le0\Rightarrow\text{fails}\)
Step 2: \(0<a<1:\ \min q=q(a)=a(2-a)>0\)
Step 3: \(a\ge1:\ q\ \text{decreasing on}\ [0,1]\Rightarrow\min q=q(1)=1-2a+2a=1>0\)
Worked derivation: \[\min_{[0,1]}q=\begin{cases}2a\le0,&a\le0\\a(2-a)>0,&0<a<1\\1,&a\ge1\end{cases}\Rightarrow a>0\]
Check: \[a=3:\ q(x)=x^2-6x+6,\ q(0)=6,\ q(1)=1,\ \text{roots}\ 3\pm\sqrt3\notin[0,1]\]
Why: \(\text{positivity is needed only on}\ [0,1],\ \text{not on}\ \mathbb R\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=3\ \text{works but is excluded}\); (B) \(a=0:\ q(0)=0\); (D) \(a=1:\ q=(x-1)^2+1>0\ \text{is excluded}\).
Key point: \(\text{compare the vertex with the interval}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Alternating falling-factorial binomial sum evaluated at a nonzero residual base
questions.syllabus_anchor: Binomial Theorem: finite expansions; differentiation
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{8}(-1)^k k(k-1)(k-2)\binom8k 2^{8-k}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) -336.
Given: \(S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^8(-1)^kk(k-1)(k-2)\binom8k2^{8-k}\)
Formula/Principle: \((2-x)^8=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^8\binom8k2^{8-k}(-1)^kx^k;\quad\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}x^k=k(k-1)(k-2)x^{k-3}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}(2-x)^8=8\cdot7\cdot6\,(-1)^3(2-x)^5=-336(2-x)^5\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}\displaystyle\sum_k(\cdots)x^k\Big|_{x=1}=S\)
Worked derivation: \[S=-336(2-1)^5=-336\]
Check: \[n=3:\ \sum_{k}(-1)^kk(k-1)(k-2)\tbinom3k2^{3-k}=(-1)^3\cdot6=-6=\frac{d^3}{dx^3}(2-x)^3\]
Why: \(\text{three derivatives give the falling factorial}\ k(k-1)(k-2)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+336\ \text{drops}\ (-1)^3\); (C) \(0=-336(2-2)^5\ \text{at}\ x=2\); (D) \(-168=-\tfrac{336}2\).
Key point: \(\text{falling factorial weights}\leftrightarrow\text{derivatives of the binomial expansion}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finite GP product reconstructed from its central term
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and Series: geometric progressions
questions.question: A real geometric progression has seven nonzero terms, and its fourth term is -2. What is the product of all seven terms?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) -128.
Given: \(a_1,\dots,a_7\ \text{in GP},\quad a_4=-2\)
Formula/Principle: \(a_j=a_4r^{\,j-4}\Rightarrow a_{4-i}\,a_{4+i}=a_4^2\)
Step 1: \(a_1a_7=a_2a_6=a_3a_5=(-2)^2=4\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^7a_j=4\cdot4\cdot4\cdot a_4\)
Worked derivation: \[\prod_{j=1}^7a_j=64\times(-2)=-128=(-2)^7\]
Check: \[r=1:\ (-2)^7=-128;\quad\prod a_4r^{\,j-4}=a_4^7r^{-3-2-1+0+1+2+3}=a_4^7\]
Why: \(\text{the exponents of}\ r\ \text{cancel in symmetric pairs}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+128\ \text{loses the sign of}\ a_4\); (B) \(-64=(-2)\cdot32\); (C) \(64=4^3\ \text{omits}\ a_4\).
Key point: \(\text{product of }2m+1\text{ GP terms}=(\text{middle term})^{2m+1}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.sub_topic: Recover laboratory launch components from two moving-camera observations
questions.syllabus_anchor: Motion in a Plane: projectile motion; relative velocity
questions.question: A camera moves horizontally at 2 m s−1 in the laboratory and is alongside a projectile at launch, with its axes remaining parallel to laboratory axes. Relative to the camera the projectile is at (6,15) m after 1 s and (12,20) m after 2 s. Air resistance is absent and g=10 m s−2. What are the laboratory launch angle above horizontal and the camera-relative horizontal coordinate when the projectile next returns to its 1-second height?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) arctan(5/2); 18 m.
Given: \(v_{\text{cam}}=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ (x),\quad(x',y)=(6,15)\ \mathrm m\ \text{at}\ 1\ \mathrm s,\ (12,20)\ \mathrm m\ \text{at}\ 2\ \mathrm s,\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(x'=(u_x-v_{\text{cam}})t,\quad y=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^2\)
Step 1: \(6=(u_x-2)(1)\Rightarrow u_x=8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(15=u_y(1)-5\Rightarrow u_y=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{u_y}{u_x}=\dfrac{20}8=\dfrac52\)
Step 4: \(20t-5t^2=15\Rightarrow t^2-4t+3=0\Rightarrow t=1\ \mathrm s,\ 3\ \mathrm s\)
Worked derivation: \[x'(3)=(8-2)(3)=18\ \mathrm m,\qquad\theta=\arctan\tfrac52\]
Check: \[t=2\ \mathrm s:\ x'=6\times2=12\ \mathrm m,\quad y=40-20=20\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(\text{the angle uses laboratory components; the coordinate asked is camera-relative}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac{20}6=\tfrac{10}3\ \text{uses}\ u_x-2\); (C) \(24\ \mathrm m=8\times3\ \text{(laboratory)}\); (D) \(\tfrac53\ne\tfrac52,\ 12\ \mathrm m=x'(2)\).
Key point: \(\vec v_{\text{rel}}=\vec v-\vec v_{\text{cam}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Zero work with a finite impulse from smooth directional reversal
questions.syllabus_anchor: Work, Energy and Power; Laws of Motion: impulse
questions.question: A 1 kg particle enters a smooth stationary U-shaped guide with velocity +2 m s−1 along x and leaves with velocity -2 m s−1 along x. The guide's force is always perpendicular to instantaneous velocity and gravity is absent. What are the work by the guide and its total x impulse on the particle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0 J and -4 N s.
Given: \(m=1\ \mathrm{kg},\quad v_{ix}=+2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad v_{fx}=-2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad\vec F\perp\vec v\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\Delta K=\tfrac12m(v_f^2-v_i^2),\quad J_x=m(v_{fx}-v_{ix})\)
Step 1: \(W=\tfrac12(1)(2^2-2^2)=0\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(J_x=(1)(-2-2)=-4\ \mathrm{N\,s}\)
Worked derivation: \[W=0\ \mathrm J,\qquad J_x=-4\ \mathrm{N\,s}\]
Check: \[P=\vec F\cdot\vec v=0\Rightarrow W=\int P\,dt=0;\quad|\Delta\vec p|=2mv=4\ \mathrm{N\,s}\]
Why: \(K\propto v^2\ \text{(no direction)};\quad\vec p\ \text{reverses}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\Delta K=0\ne4\ \mathrm J,\ J_x\ne0\); (C) \(J_x=-4\ \mathrm{N\,s}\ne0\); (D) \(W=0\ne-4\ \mathrm J\).
Key point: \(\vec F\perp\vec v:\ \text{zero work, non-zero impulse}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Off-centre impulse partitions rod energy between translation and rotation
questions.syllabus_anchor: System of Particles and Rotational Motion: angular impulse; kinetic energy
questions.question: A uniform slender rod of mass M and length L is initially at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal impulse J perpendicular to the rod is applied at a point L/6 from its centre. What fraction of the resulting total kinetic energy is rotational about the centre of mass? Use ICM=ML²/12.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/4.
Given: \(M,\ L,\quad\text{impulse}\ J\ \text{at}\ \tfrac L6\ \text{from the centre},\quad I_{CM}=\tfrac{ML^2}{12}\)
Formula/Principle: \(MV=J,\quad I_{CM}\omega=J\cdot\tfrac L6,\quad K=\tfrac12MV^2+\tfrac12I_{CM}\omega^2\)
Step 1: \(V=\dfrac JM\Rightarrow K_{tr}=\dfrac{J^2}{2M}\)
Step 2: \(\omega=\dfrac{JL/6}{ML^2/12}=\dfrac{2J}{ML}\)
Step 3: \(K_{rot}=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{ML^2}{12}\cdot\dfrac{4J^2}{M^2L^2}=\dfrac{J^2}{6M}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{tr}+K_{rot}}=\frac{\tfrac16}{\tfrac12+\tfrac16}=\frac{1/6}{4/6}=\frac14\]
Check: \[\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{tr}}=\frac{Md^2}{I_{CM}}=\frac{L^2/36}{L^2/12}=\frac13\Rightarrow\frac{1/3}{1+1/3}=\frac14\]
Why: \(\text{the impulse fixes}\ p;\ \text{its lever arm fixes}\ L_{CM}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12\Rightarrow K_{rot}=K_{tr}\ (\text{needs}\ d^2=\tfrac{L^2}{12})\); (B) \(\tfrac34=\tfrac{K_{tr}}{K}\); (D) \(\tfrac13=\tfrac{K_{rot}}{K_{tr}}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{K_{rot}}{K_{tr}}=\dfrac{Md^2}{I_{CM}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reduced-gravity capillary rise versus unchanged curvature pressure
questions.syllabus_anchor: Mechanical Properties of Fluids: surface tension; capillarity
questions.question: A clean capillary tube with fixed radius and zero contact angle gives a 4 cm rise of a liquid on Earth. The same tube and liquid are placed where gravity is g/6, with surface tension, density and contact angle unchanged and enough liquid available. Which rise and pressure jump across the meniscus follow?
options: A) 24 cm; six times the Earth pressure jump
B) 24 cm; the same pressure jump as on Earth
C) 4 cm; the same pressure jump as on Earth
D) 2/3 cm; one sixth the pressure jump
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 24 cm; the same pressure jump as on Earth.
Given: \(h=4\ \mathrm{cm},\quad\theta=0,\quad g'=\dfrac g6;\quad\gamma,\ \rho,\ r\ \text{unchanged}\)
Formula/Principle: \(h=\dfrac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{\rho gr},\quad\Delta p=\dfrac{2\gamma}r\ (\theta=0)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{h'}h=\dfrac g{g'}=6\Rightarrow h'=6\times4=24\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\Delta p'=\dfrac{2\gamma}r=\Delta p\)
Worked derivation: \[h'=24\ \mathrm{cm},\qquad\Delta p'=\Delta p\]
Check: \[\rho g'h'=\rho\cdot\frac g6\cdot6h=\rho gh=\frac{2\gamma}r\]
Why: \(\Delta p\ \text{depends only on}\ \gamma\ \text{and the curvature}\ \tfrac1r\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\Delta p'=\rho g'h'=\rho gh,\ \text{not}\ 6\rho gh\); (C) \(h\propto\tfrac1g\Rightarrow h'\ne4\ \mathrm{cm}\); (D) \(\tfrac23\ \mathrm{cm}=\tfrac h6\ (\text{inverted})\).
Key point: \(h\propto\dfrac1g;\quad\Delta p=\dfrac{2\gamma}r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Engine-driven refrigeration with a separate parasitic heat leak
questions.syllabus_anchor: Thermodynamics: Carnot engine; refrigerator; energy conservation
questions.question: A reversible engine works between 600 K and a 300 K room, absorbing 1200 J per interval. All its work drives a reversible refrigerator between that room and a 250 K cold chamber. During the same interval, 400 J also leaks from the room into the cold chamber. What are the net heat removed from the chamber and the net heat gained by the room?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2600 J and 3800 J.
Given: \(T_h=600\ \mathrm K,\ T_r=300\ \mathrm K,\ T_c=250\ \mathrm K,\ Q_h=1200\ \mathrm J,\ Q_{\text{leak}}=400\ \mathrm J\)
Formula/Principle: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_r}{T_h},\quad\mathrm{COP}=\dfrac{T_c}{T_r-T_c}\)
Step 1: \(\eta=1-\tfrac{300}{600}=0.5\Rightarrow W=0.5\times1200=600\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(Q_{\text{engine}\to\text{room}}=1200-600=600\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(\mathrm{COP}=\tfrac{250}{50}=5\Rightarrow Q_c=5\times600=3000\ \mathrm J\)
Step 4: \(Q_{\text{fridge}\to\text{room}}=3000+600=3600\ \mathrm J\)
Step 5: \(Q_{c,\text{net}}=3000-400=2600\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[Q_{\text{room,net}}=600+3600-400=3800\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[Q_h+Q_{c,\text{net}}=1200+2600=3800\ \mathrm J\ \ (\text{energy conservation})\]
Why: \(\text{the leak returns}\ 400\ \mathrm J\ \text{from the room to the chamber}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3000,\ 4200\ \text{ignore the leak}\); (B) \(4200\ne3800\ \text{(leak not subtracted from the room)}\); (C) \(2200\ne2600,\ 3400\ne3800\).
Key point: \(\text{net cooling}=\text{gross cooling}-\text{leak}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Common standing-wave frequency across a nodal density junction
questions.syllabus_anchor: Waves: string wave speed; standing waves
questions.question: Two ideal string segments, each length L, have linear densities μ and 4μ and the same tension T. Their junction and both outer ends are nodes of a normal mode. What is the lowest possible common frequency, and how many distinct nodes occur across the whole string, counting the outer ends and the junction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) √(T/μ)/(2L); four.
Given: \(\mu_1=\mu,\ \mu_2=4\mu,\ \text{length}\ L\ \text{each, tension}\ T;\quad\text{nodes at both ends and at the junction}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_i=\sqrt{\dfrac T{\mu_i}},\quad f=\dfrac{n_iv_i}{2L}\)
Step 1: \(v_1=\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu}=v,\quad v_2=\sqrt{\dfrac T{4\mu}}=\dfrac v2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{n_1v}{2L}=\dfrac{n_2v}{4L}\Rightarrow n_2=2n_1\)
Step 3: \(n_1=1,\ n_2=2\)
Step 4: \(\text{nodes}:\ (n_1+1)+(n_2+1)-1=2+3-1=4\)
Worked derivation: \[f=\frac v{2L}=\frac1{2L}\sqrt{\frac T\mu},\qquad N=4\]
Check: \[\lambda_1=\frac vf=2L,\quad\lambda_2=\frac{v/2}f=L:\quad L=1\cdot\frac{\lambda_1}2=2\cdot\frac{\lambda_2}2\]
Why: \(\text{the frequency is common; the wavelengths differ}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f=\tfrac v{4L}\Rightarrow n_1=\tfrac12\); (B) \(f=\tfrac vL\Rightarrow n_1=2,\ n_2=4\ \text{(not lowest)}\); (D) \(N=3\ \text{omits the internal node of the heavy segment}\).
Key point: \(n_2=2n_1\ \text{when}\ v_2=\tfrac{v_1}2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Global field maximum for a uniform core plus a separated shell
questions.syllabus_anchor: Gravitation: spherical mass distributions; gravitational field
questions.question: A uniform solid sphere has mass M and radius R. A concentric thin spherical shell of mass M has radius 2R. Where is the magnitude of the total gravitational field largest, and what is that maximum?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) At R; GM/R².
Given: \(\text{solid sphere}\ (M,R);\quad\text{concentric shell}\ (M,2R)\)
Formula/Principle: \(g(r)=\dfrac{GM_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2};\quad g_{\text{shell,inside}}=0\)
Step 1: \(r\le R:\ g=\dfrac{GMr}{R^3}\ (\text{increasing}),\quad g(R)=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\)
Step 2: \(R<r<2R:\ g=\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\ (\text{decreasing}),\quad g(2R^-)=\dfrac{GM}{4R^2}\)
Step 3: \(r>2R:\ g=\dfrac{2GM}{r^2},\quad g(2R^+)=\dfrac{2GM}{4R^2}=\dfrac{GM}{2R^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[g_{\max}=g(R)=\frac{GM}{R^2}>\frac{GM}{2R^2}=g(2R^+)\]
Check: \[g(0)=0;\quad g(2R^+)-g(2R^-)=\frac{GM}{4R^2}\ (\text{jump from the shell})\]
Why: \(\text{the shell adds nothing for}\ r<2R\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac{GM}{2R^2}<\tfrac{GM}{R^2}\); (C) \(g(0)=0\); (D) \(M_{\text{enc}}(R)=M,\ \text{not}\ 2M\).
Key point: \(\text{only enclosed mass contributes to}\ g\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.sub_topic: Axis-constrained stability in a quadrupole with a neutral perpendicular axis
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: potential; equilibrium
questions.question: Four fixed charges lie in the xy-plane: +q at (±a,0) and -q at (0,±a). A positive test charge is constrained in turn to move near the origin along each coordinate axis. Which local equilibrium classification is correct?
options: A) Restoring along x, unstable along y, neutral along z
B) Unstable along x, restoring along y, neutral along z
C) Restoring along every axis because potential is zero
D) Neutral along every axis because the field at the origin is zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Restoring x, unstable y, neutral z.
Given: Opposite-axis charge pairs have equal magnitudes; all charges are fixed.
Formula/Principle: Test-charge force is -Q times the potential gradient; potential curvature determines local restoring behaviour.
Step 1: Along x, \[V(x)=kq\left(\frac1{a-x}+\frac1{a+x}-\frac2{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}\right).\] Its quadratic term is \(3kqx^2/a^3\), hence \(F_x\simeq-6kqQx/a^3\).
Step 2: Interchanging x,y reverses charge signs, so the y force is anti-restoring. On the z-axis all four distances are equal and the pair fields cancel exactly.
Worked derivation: \[V_{xx}(0)=6kq/a^3>0,\quad V_{yy}(0)=-6kq/a^3<0,\quad E(0,0,z)=0.\]
Why: Zero field establishes equilibrium, not stability in every allowed direction. The curvatures can also be obtained by twice differentiating the displayed potential, without a series-convergence assumption.
Why not the others: (B) It reverses the two charged-axis curvatures. (C) A potential value does not determine its curvature. (D) It extends one-point field cancellation to nearby x and y.
Key point: State the allowed displacement direction when assessing electrostatic equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Sequential pair sharing with an isolated intermediate capacitor
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: capacitor energy; charge conservation
questions.question: Three equal isolated capacitors A,B,C each have capacitance C0. Initially A has voltage V and B,C are uncharged. First A and B are connected positive plate to positive plate through a resistor until equilibrium. They are disconnected, leaving B isolated. Then A is connected similarly to C until equilibrium. What are B's final voltage and the total heat dissipated in the two resistors?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) V/2; 5C0V²/16.
Given: \(C_A=C_B=C_C=C_0;\quad V_A=V,\ V_B=V_C=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(V_{\text{common}}=\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{C_1+C_2},\quad H=U_i-U_f,\quad U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(\text{A–B}:\ V_1=\dfrac{C_0V+0}{2C_0}=\dfrac V2\Rightarrow V_B=\dfrac V2\ (\text{then isolated})\)
Step 2: \(\text{A–C}:\ V_2=\dfrac{C_0(V/2)+0}{2C_0}=\dfrac V4\)
Step 3: \(U_i=\tfrac12C_0V^2\)
Step 4: \(U_f=\tfrac12C_0\left[\left(\tfrac V2\right)^2+2\left(\tfrac V4\right)^2\right]=\tfrac12C_0V^2\cdot\tfrac38=\tfrac3{16}C_0V^2\)
Worked derivation: \[H=\tfrac12C_0V^2-\tfrac3{16}C_0V^2=\tfrac5{16}C_0V^2,\qquad V_B=\tfrac V2\]
Check: \[H_1=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{C_0}2V^2=\tfrac14C_0V^2,\quad H_2=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{C_0}2\left(\tfrac V2\right)^2=\tfrac1{16}C_0V^2,\quad H_1+H_2=\tfrac5{16}C_0V^2\]
Why: \(\text{B is isolated during the second connection}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac V3\ \text{needs all three connected together}\); (B) \(\tfrac V4=V_A=V_C\ne V_B\); (C) \(\tfrac14C_0V^2=H_1\ \text{only}\).
Key point: \(H=\tfrac12\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}(\Delta V)^2\ \text{for each connection}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Load threshold reverses current in a weaker parallel cell
questions.syllabus_anchor: Current Electricity: cells; internal resistance; Kirchhoff's rules
questions.question: Cells of emf 12 V and 6 V, each with internal resistance 1 ohm, are connected in parallel with their positive terminals joined and a load R across the common terminals. What load resistance marks zero current in the 6 V cell, and what charging current enters that cell when R=2 ohm?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1 ohm; 6/5 A.
Given: \(E_1=12\ \mathrm V,\ E_2=6\ \mathrm V,\ r_1=r_2=1\ \Omega;\quad\text{load}\ R\ \text{across the common terminals (voltage}\ U)\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_k=\dfrac{E_k-U}{r_k},\quad I_1+I_2=\dfrac UR\)
Step 1: \((12-U)+(6-U)=\dfrac UR\Rightarrow U=\dfrac{18R}{2R+1}\)
Step 2: \(I_2=0\Rightarrow U=6\ \mathrm V:\ 18R=12R+6\Rightarrow R=1\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(R=2\ \Omega:\ U=\dfrac{36}5=7.2\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[I_{\text{charge}}=\frac{U-E_2}{r_2}=\frac{7.2-6}1=\frac65\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[I_1=12-7.2=4.8\ \mathrm A,\quad I_R=\frac{7.2}2=3.6\ \mathrm A,\quad4.8=3.6+1.2\]
Why: \(U>E_2\Rightarrow\text{current enters the positive terminal of the 6 V cell}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(R=2\ \Omega\Rightarrow U=7.2\ \mathrm V\ne6\ \mathrm V\); (C) \(\tfrac{18}5\ \mathrm A=I_R\); (D) \(R=\tfrac12\ \Omega\Rightarrow U=4.5\ \mathrm V\ne6\ \mathrm V\).
Key point: \(\text{a cell is charged when the terminal voltage exceeds its emf}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Magnetic-stripe width decides return rather than transmission
questions.syllabus_anchor: Moving Charges and Magnetism: charged-particle circular motion
questions.question: A positive particle enters at x=0 with velocity v along +x into a uniform magnetic field +B along z confined to 0<x<d. Let R=mv/(qB) and take d=3R/2. With no other forces, through which boundary does it leave, after what time, and in what direction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It returns through the left boundary after half a cyclotron period, moving -x.
Given: The stripe is wider than the orbit's maximum x penetration.
Formula/Principle: The magnetic force turns velocity clockwise in the xy-plane with angular speed Ω=qB/m.
Step 1: Taking the entry point as origin, \[x=R\sin\Omega t,\quad y=R(\cos\Omega t-1).\] Maximum x is R, less than d=1.5R, so it never reaches the right boundary.
Step 2: The first subsequent x=0 occurs at Ωt=π. Its velocity is \((v\cos\pi,-v\sin\pi)=(-v,0)\).
Worked derivation: \[t=\pi m/(qB),\quad \mathbf v_{exit}=-v\hat x.\]
Why: Finite-field trajectories must be checked against the boundary before assuming transmission.
Why not the others: (A) The right boundary lies beyond maximum penetration. (C) It also assumes impossible transmission. (D) The particle exits after half a turn, not a full turn.
Key point: Compare magnetic radius with stripe width to decide exit topology.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Capacitor-voltage peak differs from series-current resonance
questions.syllabus_anchor: Alternating Current: series LCR response; resonance
questions.question: A series RLC circuit is driven by a sinusoidal source of fixed voltage amplitude E. L=1 H, C=0.010 F and R=10 ohm. At what angular frequency is the capacitor voltage amplitude greatest, and what is that greatest amplitude divided by E?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5√2 rad s−1; 2/√3.
Given: \(L=1\ \mathrm H,\quad C=0.010\ \mathrm F,\quad R=10\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{V_C}E=\dfrac{X_C}Z=\dfrac1{\sqrt{(1-\omega^2LC)^2+\omega^2R^2C^2}}\)
Step 1: \(LC=0.010\ \mathrm{s^2},\quad R^2C^2=100\times10^{-4}=0.010\ \mathrm{s^2}\)
Step 2: \(u=\omega^2:\ D(u)=(1-0.01u)^2+0.01u\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dD}{du}=-0.02(1-0.01u)+0.01=0\Rightarrow1-0.01u=\tfrac12\Rightarrow u=50\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}\)
Step 4: \(D_{\min}=\left(\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac12=\tfrac34\)
Worked derivation: \[\omega=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\qquad\frac{V_C}E=\frac1{\sqrt{3/4}}=\frac2{\sqrt3}\approx1.155\]
Check: \[\omega=10:\ D=0+1=1\Rightarrow\frac{V_C}E=1<1.155;\quad\omega^2=\frac1{LC}-\frac{R^2}{2L^2}=100-50=50\]
Why: \(V_C=IX_C\ \text{and}\ X_C\ \text{falls with}\ \omega\Rightarrow\text{the peak lies below}\ \omega_0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\omega=10:\ \tfrac{V_C}E=1\ (\text{current resonance})\); (B) \(\omega=10:\ 1\ne\sqrt2\); (D) \(\omega=5:\ D=0.5625+0.25=0.8125\Rightarrow1.109\ne2\).
Key point: \(\omega_{V_C\max}^2=\dfrac1{LC}-\dfrac{R^2}{2L^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fixed-lens microscope refocusing from infinity to a finite virtual image
questions.syllabus_anchor: Ray Optics: microscope; lens formula
questions.question: A compound microscope has objective focal length 1 cm, eyepiece focal length 5 cm and lens separation 11 cm. Initially the final image is at infinity. Keeping both lenses fixed, the object is moved until the eyepiece forms a virtual final image 25 cm from it on its incident side. What is the new object distance from the objective, and how far and in which direction was it moved?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 41/35 cm; 1/35 cm toward.
Given: \(f_o=1\ \mathrm{cm},\quad f_e=5\ \mathrm{cm},\quad d=11\ \mathrm{cm},\quad v_e=-25\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f\)
Step 1: \(\text{image at}\ \infty:\ |u_e|=5\ \mathrm{cm}\Rightarrow v_o=11-5=6\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac1{u_o}=\dfrac16-1=-\dfrac56\Rightarrow|u_o|=\dfrac65\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac1{u_e}=\dfrac1{-25}-\dfrac15=-\dfrac6{25}\Rightarrow|u_e|=\dfrac{25}6\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 4: \(v_o'=11-\dfrac{25}6=\dfrac{41}6\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 5: \(\dfrac1{u_o'}=\dfrac6{41}-1=-\dfrac{35}{41}\Rightarrow|u_o'|=\dfrac{41}{35}\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac65-\frac{41}{35}=\frac{42-41}{35}=\frac1{35}\ \mathrm{cm}\ \ (\text{toward the objective})\]
Check: \[\frac{35}{41}+\frac6{41}=1=\frac1{f_o};\quad\frac6{25}-\frac1{25}=\frac15=\frac1{f_e}\]
Why: \(\text{a nearer final image needs a longer}\ v_o,\ \text{so a shorter}\ |u_o|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac65\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{is the initial distance}\); (C) \(\tfrac{41}{35}<\tfrac{42}{35}\Rightarrow\text{toward, not away}\); (D) \(\tfrac{35}{41}\ \mathrm{cm}<f_o\Rightarrow\text{no real intermediate image}\).
Key point: \(\text{work back from the eyepiece to the objective}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Counterpropagating electromagnetic fields and failure of a single-wave field ratio
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electromagnetic Waves: transverse fields; energy transport; superposition
questions.question: Two equal plane electromagnetic waves in vacuum have electric fields \(E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat y\) and \(E_0\cos(kx+\omega t)\hat y\). Their magnetic fields point along +z and -z, respectively, for positive values of the corresponding cosine. At x=0, which total fields and comparison with the single-travelling-wave relation E=cB are correct?
options: A) E=0 and B=2E0 cos(ωt)/c; magnetic fields add
B) E=2E0 cos(ωt) along y and B=E/c along z; the single-wave ratio remains valid
C) Both fields vanish at all times; no electric field remains
D) E=2E0 cos(ωt) along y and B=0; their sum generally does not obey the single-wave ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) E=2E0 cos(ωt) along y and B=0; their sum generally does not obey the single-wave ratio.
Given: \(\vec E_1=E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat y,\ \vec B_1=\dfrac{E_0}c\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat z;\quad\vec E_2=E_0\cos(kx+\omega t)\hat y,\ \vec B_2=-\dfrac{E_0}c\cos(kx+\omega t)\hat z\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec E=\vec E_1+\vec E_2,\quad\vec B=\vec B_1+\vec B_2\)
Step 1: \(x=0:\ \cos(-\omega t)=\cos(\omega t)\)
Step 2: \(\vec E=2E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat y\)
Step 3: \(\vec B=\dfrac{E_0}c\cos(\omega t)\hat z-\dfrac{E_0}c\cos(\omega t)\hat z=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec E(0,t)=2E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat y,\qquad\vec B(0,t)=0\Rightarrow E\ne cB\]
Check: \[\vec E=2E_0\cos kx\cos\omega t\,\hat y,\quad\vec B=\frac{2E_0}c\sin kx\sin\omega t\,\hat z:\ x=0\Rightarrow B=0\]
Why: \(E=cB\ \text{holds for each travelling wave, not for their standing-wave sum}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(E\ \text{and}\ B\ \text{interchanged}\); (B) \(B=0\ne\tfrac Ec\); (C) \(E=2E_0\cos\omega t\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{in a standing EM wave the}\ E\ \text{antinodes are}\ B\ \text{nodes}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Atomic-to-nuclear mass conversion before the positron threshold
questions.syllabus_anchor: Nuclei: atomic masses; radioactivity; mass-energy relation
questions.question: Neutral-atom masses of a parent (A,Z) and daughter (A,Z-1) differ by 1.5 electron masses, the parent being heavier. Neglect electronic binding, nuclear excitation and neutrino mass. What is the corresponding bare-nucleus mass difference, and is spontaneous positron emission energetically possible?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.5 me; impossible.
Given: \(M_P^{\text{atom}}-M_D^{\text{atom}}=1.5\,m_e;\quad(A,Z)\to(A,Z-1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(M^{\text{nuc}}=M^{\text{atom}}-Zm_e;\quad Q_{\beta^+}=\left(M_P^{\text{nuc}}-M_D^{\text{nuc}}-m_e\right)c^2\)
Step 1: \(M_P^{\text{nuc}}-M_D^{\text{nuc}}=\left(M_P^{\text{atom}}-Zm_e\right)-\left(M_D^{\text{atom}}-(Z-1)m_e\right)\)
Step 2: \(=1.5\,m_e-m_e=0.5\,m_e\)
Worked derivation: \[Q_{\beta^+}=(0.5-1)\,m_ec^2=-0.5\,m_ec^2<0\Rightarrow\text{not possible}\]
Check: \[Q_{\beta^+}=\left(\Delta M^{\text{atom}}-2m_e\right)c^2=(1.5-2)\,m_ec^2=-0.5\,m_ec^2\]
Why: \(\beta^+\ \text{decay needs}\ \Delta M^{\text{atom}}>2m_e\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1.5\,m_e\ \text{is the atomic, not nuclear, difference}\); (B) \(1.5+1=2.5\ (\text{wrong sign})\); (D) \(0.5\,m_e<m_e\Rightarrow Q<0\).
Key point: \(Q_{\beta^+}=\left(M_P^{\text{atom}}-M_D^{\text{atom}}-2m_e\right)c^2\)
